warmup.q: fun requirePaper(paper: String?) { if (paper == null) throw IllegalArgumentException() }. After requirePaper(paper), where paper is a String?, you write paper.uppercase(). What happens?
options: It compiles: the compiler sees the throw inside requirePaper
Compile error: paper is still a String? to the compiler
It compiles, and throws NullPointerException if paper is null
warmup.why: The compiler decides smart casts one function at a time. It doesn't look inside requirePaper to learn that a normal return means paper != null, so paper stays nullable and you get only safe (?.) or non-null asserted (!!.) calls are allowed on a nullable receiver of type 'String?'. The standard library's require gets the smart cast because it declares a contract, the subject of the first section.

opening:
At the print shop, jobs travel between desks in envelopes. A clerk who opens an envelope and sees a paper size written inside knows the job has one. The next clerk down the line doesn't know that, and she would have to open the envelope again. Unless the first clerk stamps the outside: "checked, paper size filled in". Then the next clerk trusts the stamp and gets on with the job.

The Kotlin compiler works the same way. It knows what it saw in the function it is reading, and it never opens a function you call, so your own check function, however careful, teaches it nothing. A contract is the stamp on the outside. The easy trap is the other half of the story: nobody checks a stamp. The compiler believes it, true or not.

In the last lesson we wrote a small language and saw context receivers retire. This time we stamp our own envelopes, watch a false stamp fail at run time, and meet context parameters, the values every clerk on a shift carries without being handed them on each job. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with envelopes moving between desks. A contract is the stamp on the outside, returns() implies or callsInPlace, and the compiler believes it without opening the envelope, so a false stamp turns into a ClassCastException later. Context parameters are what every clerk carries for the whole shift: passed by the compiler, and on the JVM as plain leading parameters.

In your own code, look for a check function followed by !! on the next line. Each one is a missing contract, or a hint that the check should return the value instead.

Next, we'll let the compiler change our classes as they pass through it. What do compiler plugins write into a class file that your source never mentions?

sections.h: Your own check functions teach the compiler nothing, until they carry a contract
sections.html:
Start with a check the print shop's app makes all the time. Some printers report their paper size and some don't, so lookupPaper("laser-1") returns a String?: a paper size such as "a4", or null, Kotlin's word for no value at all. Before printing, the app must be sure there is one. The standard library's require(paper != null) does that, and on the next line paper can be used as a plain String. Write the same check as your own function, and the compiler forgets it:

Java
// Java's type system doesn't track null at all, so the question never comes up
static void requirePaper(String paper) {
    if (paper == null) throw new IllegalArgumentException("paper size missing");
}

requirePaper(paper);
System.out.println(paper.toUpperCase());      // compiles, as everything does
Kotlin
fun requirePaperPlain(paper: String?) {
    if (paper == null) throw IllegalArgumentException("paper size missing")
}

requirePaperPlain(paper)
println(paper.uppercase())
// error: only safe (?.) or non-null asserted (!!.) calls are allowed on a nullable receiver of type 'String?'.

The feature that fails here is the smart cast: after a check such as if (paper != null), the compiler treats paper as the narrower type, String, without a cast written by you. It does that only for checks it can see in the function it is reading. It never reads the body of a function you call.

In the print shop, the compiler is a clerk who trusts her own eyes. She saw the check? Then she knows. A colleague did it at another desk? Then, as far as she is concerned, it never happened.

A contract is the stamp on the outside of the envelope. It is a contract { } block, written as the first statement of a function, that states a fact about the function's behavior for callers to rely on. Two kinds matter in practice. returns() implies (paper != null) says: if this function returns normally, the condition holds. callsInPlace(block, InvocationKind.EXACTLY_ONCE) says: the lambda runs exactly once, during this call, and is never kept for later. The other counts are AT_MOST_ONCE, AT_LEAST_ONCE and UNKNOWN.

Java
// Java can't assign a local inside a lambda at all:
// "local variables referenced from a lambda expression must be final or effectively final"
String[] label = new String[1];
ContractsDemoKt.once(() -> { label[0] = "job-17"; return Unit.INSTANCE; });
Kotlin
@OptIn(ExperimentalContracts::class)
fun requirePaper(paper: String?) {
    contract { returns() implies (paper != null) }
    if (paper == null) throw IllegalArgumentException("paper size missing")
}

@OptIn(ExperimentalContracts::class)
inline fun <T> once(block: () -> T): T {
    contract { callsInPlace(block, InvocationKind.EXACTLY_ONCE) }
    return block()
}

val label: String
once { label = "job-17" }     // allowed: the block runs exactly once

With the contract, requirePaper(paper) can be followed by paper.uppercase(), and the demo prints paper = A4. With once, a val declared without a value can be assigned inside the lambda, because the compiler now knows the lambda runs exactly once, before the next line. Take the callsInPlace line out, and being inline (pasted into the caller, as lesson 1 showed) isn't enough. You get 'val' cannot be reassigned. and variable 'label' must be initialized., because an inline function may still call its lambda twice, or not at all.

This is how require, check, requireNotNull, run, let and apply work in the standard library. Contracts are still Experimental in Kotlin 2.4, which means the feature may still change and you must agree to use it in writing. The 2.4.0 release notes say so, and without @OptIn(ExperimentalContracts::class) every part of the block fails with this declaration needs opt-in. No compiler flag is needed, only that annotation.

The compiler smart-casts only from checks it can see. A contract writes the check on the outside of the function.

So the clerk trusts the stamp. The next question is whether she should.

try.title: Take each contract away
steps: Run ContractsDemo (or ContractsDemoJava, which calls the same Kotlin functions).
Wrong move 1: call requirePaperPlain(paper) instead of requirePaper(paper). Predict the error, run, undo.
Wrong move 2: delete the contract { callsInPlace(...) } line in once. once is still inline. Predict whether that is enough, run, undo.
Wrong move 3: delete the @OptIn above isPrinted, run, undo.

code.title: ContractsDemo.kt
code.html: package workbench.kotlin.l05.demo import kotlin.contracts.ExperimentalContracts import kotlin.contracts.InvocationKind import kotlin.contracts.contract sealed interface JobEvent data class Printed(val jobId: String, val pages: Int) : JobEvent data class Jammed(val jobId: String, val printer: String) : JobEvent fun lookupPaper(printer: String): String? = if (printer.startsWith("laser-")) "a4" else null /** Checks, but tells the compiler nothing. */ fun requirePaperPlain(paper: String?) { if (paper == null) throw IllegalArgumentException("paper size missing") } /** The same check, plus a promise: if this returns, paper was not null. */ @OptIn(ExperimentalContracts::class) fun requirePaper(paper: String?) { contract { returns() implies (paper != null) } if (paper == null) throw IllegalArgumentException("paper size missing") } /** A promise about the receiver: a true result means this is a Printed. */ @OptIn(ExperimentalContracts::class) fun JobEvent.isPrinted(): Boolean { contract { returns(true) implies (this@isPrinted is Printed) } return this is Printed } /** A promise about the lambda: it runs exactly once, during this call. */ @OptIn(ExperimentalContracts::class) inline fun <T> once(block: () -> T): T { contract { callsInPlace(block, InvocationKind.EXACTLY_ONCE) } return block() } fun main() { val paper = lookupPaper("laser-1") requirePaper(paper) println("paper = ${paper.uppercase()}") // smart cast to String val event: JobEvent = Printed("job-7", 12) if (event.isPrinted()) println("printed ${event.pages} pages") // smart cast to Printed val label: String // a val, assigned inside a lambda once { label = "job-17" } println("label = $label") // Wrong moves, one at a time. Predict the error, run, undo. // 1. Call requirePaperPlain(paper) instead of requirePaper(paper). // 2. Delete the line `contract { callsInPlace(...) }` in once. // 3. Delete @OptIn(ExperimentalContracts::class) above isPrinted. }

alt.title: ContractsDemoJava.java
alt.html: package workbench.kotlin.l05.demo; import kotlin.Unit; /** * Java twin of ContractsDemo.kt. Java has no contracts. It has no null checks in the type system to * satisfy, its instanceof pattern binds a new variable instead of smart-casting, and a lambda may * not assign a local variable at all. */ public class ContractsDemoJava { public static void main(String[] args) { String paper = ContractsDemoKt.lookupPaper("laser-1"); ContractsDemoKt.requirePaper(paper); // to Java: a void method, nothing more System.out.println("paper = " + paper.toUpperCase()); JobEvent event = new Printed("job-7", 12); if (event instanceof Printed p) { // the pattern binds p: no promise needed System.out.println("printed " + p.getPages() + " pages"); } // String label; once(() -> { label = "x"; ... }) would not compile: // "local variables referenced from a lambda expression must be final or effectively final" String[] label = new String[1]; ContractsDemoKt.once(() -> { label[0] = "job-17"; return Unit.INSTANCE; }); System.out.println("label = " + label[0]); } }

Move 2 fails with 'val' cannot be reassigned. and variable 'label' must be initialized.: being inline doesn't tell the compiler how many times the body calls block. Move 3 fails with this declaration needs opt-in. Its usage must be marked with '@kotlin.contracts.ExperimentalContracts' or '@OptIn(kotlin.contracts.ExperimentalContracts::class)'.

aside.title: Why doesn't the compiler just read the body of the function?
aside.html: Because then a change inside one function could break code far away. Today a function's signature, its parameter and return types, is the promise callers rely on, and the body is free to change. If smart casts followed bodies, deleting the throw from requirePaper would silently change which callers compile, perhaps in a module built months ago. Often the body isn't there to read anyway: a library arrives as compiled class files, and the compiler reads their signatures, not their code. A contract keeps the promise next to the signature, written down on purpose, where a reviewer can see it.

video.title: The compiler smart-casts only from checks it can see; a contract is the stamp on the outside of the envelope, believed and never checked

sections.h: The compiler trusts a contract and never checks it
sections.html:
A contract is a promise, and nothing checks the body against it. The design document for contracts, KEEP-139, says the compiler "trusts contracts unconditionally" and that the programmer is "responsible for writing correct and sound contracts". Proving the body right is listed as a non-goal.

The demo's job events say what happened to a print job: Printed(jobId, pages) when it came out of the printer, and Jammed(jobId, printer) when it got stuck, which laser-1 does now and then. isPrinted() answers whether an event is a Printed, and its contract lets the caller read event.pages right after a true. The lying version answers true to everything, like a clerk who stamps every envelope unopened. It's very fast work. It also compiles without a single warning:

Java
// Java's version of the same lie: a check that always says yes, and a cast that believes it
static boolean lyingIsPrinted(JobEvent e) { return true; }

if (lyingIsPrinted(jammed)) {
    Printed p = (Printed) jammed;                  // ClassCastException
}
Kotlin
@OptIn(ExperimentalContracts::class)
fun JobEvent.lyingIsPrinted(): Boolean {
    contract { returns(true) implies (this@lyingIsPrinted is Printed) }
    return true                                    // the lie
}

if (jammed.lyingIsPrinted()) println(jammed.pages)   // ClassCastException

The smart cast to Printed lets jammed.pages compile. At run time the JVM still checks every cast it is given, and a Jammed is not a Printed: class ...Jammed cannot be cast to class ...Printed. A contract can't make a wrong value right. It only moves the cast out of your code, where a reviewer would see it, into a promise inside another function.

One level down, the reason is plain. javap -c on the honest isPrinted shows a null check on the receiver, then instanceof Printed and ireturn, with no trace of the contract. The smart cast lands in the caller instead: right after the call, javap shows a checkcast Printed that nobody wrote by hand. The contract itself lives in the Kotlin metadata of the class file, extra data that only the Kotlin compiler reads when it compiles a caller. Java never sees it, and nothing in the running program enforces it.

The K2 compiler (the current Kotlin compiler, the default since Kotlin 2.0) does catch some callsInPlace mistakes, as warnings. A block declared EXACTLY_ONCE but called twice gets wrong invocation kind 'EXACTLY_ONCE' for 'block: () -> Unit' specified, the actual invocation kind is 'AT_LEAST_ONCE'. A block declared in place but kept in a list gets leaked in-place lambda 'block: () -> Unit'. Nothing checks returns ... implies. The one firm rule is the position: any statement before the block is an error, contract should be the first statement.

A contract is believed, never checked. Keep the body as simple as the promise.

So write contracts the way the standard library does: tiny functions whose body is the condition itself, such as if (!condition) throw ..., so that a reader can check the promise at a glance. Kotlin 2.2.20 added more Experimental forms, such as contracts on property getters, returnsNotNull() and holdsIn. The last two need a second opt-in, ExperimentalExtendedContracts.

Contracts tell the compiler what a function does. The next feature is about what a function needs, and it changes how arguments get passed.

steps: Run LyingContractDemo. Before you do, predict: compile error, a warning, or a run-time failure?
Run LyingContractDemoJava, which tells the same lie in Java with a cast, then calls the Kotlin function.
Run javap -c -p -cp kotlin/build/classes/kotlin/demo workbench.kotlin.l05.demo.ContractsDemoKt from labs/. Read isPrinted, then find the checkcast in main right after the call to it.

code.title: LyingContractDemo.kt
code.html: package workbench.kotlin.l05.demo import kotlin.contracts.ExperimentalContracts import kotlin.contracts.contract /** A contract that lies. The compiler checks neither the promise nor the body. */ @OptIn(ExperimentalContracts::class) fun JobEvent.lyingIsPrinted(): Boolean { contract { returns(true) implies (this@lyingIsPrinted is Printed) } return true } fun main() { val jammed: JobEvent = Jammed("job-8", "laser-1") try { if (jammed.lyingIsPrinted()) println("printed ${jammed.pages} pages") } catch (e: ClassCastException) { println("ClassCastException: ${e.message}") } }

alt.title: LyingContractDemoJava.java
alt.html: package workbench.kotlin.l05.demo; /** * Java twin of LyingContractDemo.kt. Java's version of the same lie is a helper that answers true * and a cast that trusts it. In both languages the cast is the line that fails at run time. */ public class LyingContractDemoJava { static boolean lyingIsPrinted(JobEvent e) { return true; } public static void main(String[] args) { JobEvent jammed = new Jammed("job-8", "laser-1"); try { if (lyingIsPrinted(jammed)) { Printed p = (Printed) jammed; // Java makes you write the cast yourself System.out.println("printed " + p.getPages() + " pages"); } } catch (ClassCastException e) { System.out.println("ClassCastException: " + e.getMessage()); } // the Kotlin function, seen from Java: just a boolean method, the contract is gone System.out.println("Kotlin lyingIsPrinted from Java: " + LyingContractDemoKt.lyingIsPrinted(jammed)); } }

try.expect: It compiles cleanly and fails at run time with ClassCastException: class workbench.kotlin.l05.demo.Jammed cannot be cast to class workbench.kotlin.l05.demo.Printed. The Java twin fails the same way, then prints Kotlin lyingIsPrinted from Java: true: to Java it's a boolean method. In javap, isPrinted is a null check on the receiver, then instanceof and ireturn, with no contract in sight. In main, the call to isPrinted is followed by checkcast Printed and getPages: that cast is the smart cast.

sections.h: Context parameters: what every clerk carries for the whole shift
sections.html:
Some values must reach almost every function that handles a job. In the print shop, every decision goes into the shift's logbook, and every line in it starts with the name of the shift on duty, such as [early]. Passed by hand, the logbook and the shift show up in every signature, whether the function uses them or only hands them on:

Java
static boolean check(Logbook logbook, Shift shift, Job job, String printer) {
    logbook.write("[" + shift.name() + "] checking " + job.copies() + " copies of " + job.file() + " for " + printer);
    return job.copies() <= 1_000;
}

static String takeIn(Logbook logbook, Shift shift, Job job, String printer) {
    boolean ok = check(logbook, shift, job, printer);     // pass both on, by hand
    remark(logbook, job.file() + (ok ? " accepted" : " refused") + " on the " + shift.name() + " shift");
    return ok ? "ACCEPTED" : "REFUSED";
}
Kotlin
context(logbook: Logbook, shift: Shift)
fun Job.check(printer: String): Boolean {
    logbook.write("[${shift.name}] checking $copies copies of $file for $printer")
    return copies <= 1_000
}

context(logbook: Logbook, shift: Shift)
fun takeIn(job: Job, printer: String): String {
    val ok = job.check(printer)                           // logbook and shift flow on by themselves
    remark("${job.file} ${if (ok) "accepted" else "refused"} on the ${shift.name} shift")
    return if (ok) "ACCEPTED" else "REFUSED"
}

The Kotlin version declares the two values once per function, in context(...) before fun, and stops passing them. A context parameter is a parameter the caller doesn't write. You declare it with a name and a type, and inside the function you use it by its name, as check does with logbook and shift. At each call, the compiler looks for a value of that type in the caller's surroundings and passes it for you. The value it finds is called the context argument.

In the print shop, the context parameters are what every clerk on a shift carries: the shift's logbook and the shift's name. Nobody hands them over with each job. The demo hands them out once, at the start of the shift, with context(console, Shift("early")) { ... }, and inside that block every function that needs them has them.

The compiler finds a context argument in one of three places. The first is an enclosing function's own context parameter, as takeIn passes its logbook and shift on to check. The second is a context(a, b) { ... } block from the standard library. The third is an implicit receiver, such as the this of a with(console) { ... } block. If you don't need a name, write _ and read the value with contextOf<Logbook>(), as the demo's remark does. Forget the context altogether, and the call doesn't compile: no context argument for 'logbook: Logbook' found.

The docs describe context parameters as dependencies that are "implicitly available in the surrounding context". On the JVM nothing about them is implicit, as the figure shows. They become ordinary leading parameters: the context parameters first, then the extension receiver, then the value parameters. javap prints check(Logbook, Shift, Job, String), and Java calls it by passing all four. That's where the shift picture breaks. On the JVM the clerk is handed the logbook with every single job, and a Java caller hands it over in person, every time.

The status changed fast, so here it is plainly. Context parameters replaced context receivers, the experiment from the last lesson. Context receivers arrived in Kotlin 1.6.20 as a prototype behind -Xcontext-receivers. Kotlin 2.2.0 brought context parameters as a preview, a feature you can try but which may still change, behind -Xcontext-parameters. Kotlin 2.3.20 removed context receivers. Kotlin 2.4.0 made context parameters Stable, "except for context arguments and callable references", two parts the next section covers. So in Kotlin 2.4 you need no flag, and an old build file that still passes one earns warning: the argument '-Xcontext-parameters' is redundant for the current language version 2.4.

The two designs differ in one way that matters when you read older code. A context receiver had no name and acted like an extra this, so you called its members bare, as in write("hi"). A context parameter has a name, and you write logbook.write("hi").

A context parameter is an argument the compiler finds by type and passes for you. On the JVM, it is a plain leading parameter.

Finding a value by type works well while there is exactly one candidate. The next section is about the other cases.

sections.h: Finding values by type: ambiguity, limits, and where context parameters fit
sections.html:
The compiler finds context arguments by type, so two values of the same type in the same place are a problem. Take a smaller note that needs only a logbook, context(logbook: Logbook) fun note(line: String). Put the front desk's logbook and the back room's logbook in one block, context(front, back) { note("x") }, and the compiler won't pick one: multiple potential context arguments for 'logbook: Logbook' in scope. The docs give the rule: if several compatible values exist at the same scope level, the compiler reports an ambiguity. A nearer scope still wins over an outer one. In context(front) { context(back) { note("x") } }, the inner back is used, and the line goes to the back room.

That's a reason to give context parameters specific types: a Shift class instead of a bare String, a Logbook interface instead of a (String) -> Unit function type. A bare String in a context would match any string in scope.

A few things are not allowed. Constructors can't have context parameters: context parameters on primary constructors are unsupported. A property can have them only if it has no backing field, the hidden field that stores a property's value, so it must be a computed getter: property with context parameters cannot be initialized because it has no backing field. And two parts are still not stable in Kotlin 2.4. One is passing a context argument by name, as in note(logbook = front, line = "x"), an Experimental feature behind -Xexplicit-context-arguments. Without the flag, 2.4.21 says it "is only available since language version 2.5". The other is a callable reference, ::note, which fails with callable reference to 'context(logbook: Logbook) fun note(line: String): Unit' is unsupported because it has context parameters. Leave both alone for now.

One change in Kotlin 2.3.20 can surprise you if you bring older preview code forward. Overload resolution, the compiler's choice between functions with the same name, used to prefer a function with context parameters over one without. The 2.3.20 notes say that rule no longer applies, so two overloads that differ only by a context may now be ambiguous.

The JVM shape has two more consequences. Java can call these functions, as long as it passes every argument itself. And adding a context parameter to a public function changes its JVM signature exactly as adding any parameter does, so code compiled against the old version fails with NoSuchMethodError. Treat it as a change to the function's public API.

So where do context parameters fit? Not for the long-lived helpers an object is built with: a paper catalogue or a printer driver belongs in the constructor, passed once. Context parameters suit values that belong to the current piece of work and are needed by many small functions: the shift, its logbook, the id of the job in hand, a clock that tests can stop. They are visible in every signature, and the compiler checks them, which a hidden global value never does.

That's also the limit of both tools in this lesson. A contract is believed without checks, and a context argument is found by its type, never by its meaning. Keeping either honest is your job.

A check to finish, with the lab's review, which needs a Logbook and a Shift: with(Logbook { println(it) }) { context(Shift("late")) { JobRequest(40, "a3", "poster.pdf").review(1_000) } }. Will it compile, and where does each context argument come from? (It compiles. The Logbook comes from the implicit receiver of with, and the Shift from the context(...) block. Each type has exactly one candidate.)

compare.title: A job review with a logbook: Java parameters vs Kotlin contracts and context parameters

java.title: Review.java
java.html: final class Review { static void ensure(boolean condition, String code, Supplier<String> message) { if (!condition) throw new JobRejected(code, message.get()); } static Decision review(Logbook logbook, Shift shift, JobRequest job, int maxCopies) { try { ensure(job.copies() <= maxCopies, "TOO_MANY", () -> "over the limit"); ensure(job.paper() != null, "PAPER_MISSING", () -> "a paper size is required"); logbook.write("[" + shift.name() + "] accepted " + job.paper().toUpperCase()); return Decision.ACCEPTED; } catch (JobRejected e) { logbook.write("[" + shift.name() + "] rejected " + e.code()); return Decision.rejected(e.code()); } } }

kotlin.title: Review.kt
kotlin.html: @OptIn(ExperimentalContracts::class) inline fun ensure(condition: Boolean, code: String, lazyMessage: () -> String) { contract { returns() implies condition callsInPlace(lazyMessage, InvocationKind.AT_MOST_ONCE) } if (!condition) throw JobRejected(code, lazyMessage()) } context(logbook: Logbook, shift: Shift) fun JobRequest.review(maxCopies: Int): Decision = try { ensure(copies <= maxCopies, "TOO_MANY") { "over the limit" } ensure(paper != null, "PAPER_MISSING") { "a paper size is required" } logbook.write("[${shift.name}] accepted ${paper.uppercase()}") // smart cast Decision.Accepted } catch (e: JobRejected) { logbook.write("[${shift.name}] rejected ${e.code}") Decision.Rejected(e.code) }

compare.note: The Java version compiles because Java doesn't track null, so job.paper().toUpperCase() is accepted whether or not the check ran. The Kotlin version compiles only because the contract tells the compiler that ensure returns only when its condition holds. Kotlin's ensure is inline, so the message lambda costs nothing when the check passes, while Java builds a Supplier on every call. The logbook and the shift appear in Java's signature as two extra parameters that every caller passes on. In Kotlin they are context parameters, filled in by the compiler, and they still compile to exactly those two leading parameters, so Java can call the Kotlin review as review(logbook, shift, job, maxCopies).

worked.title: Replace a ThreadLocal shift name with a context parameter

steps.say: The app keeps the current shift's name in a ThreadLocal, a variable that holds one value per thread, so that deep helpers can write it into the logbook. It works until a helper runs on another thread, or a test forgets to set it, and then the logbook says [null]. The compiler can't help, because nothing in any signature says the value is needed.
steps.code: final class CurrentShift { static final ThreadLocal<String> NAME = new ThreadLocal<>(); } static void note(String line) { System.out.println("[" + CurrentShift.NAME.get() + "] " + line); // null if nobody set it }

alt.html: object CurrentShift { val name = ThreadLocal<String>() } fun note(line: String) { println("[${CurrentShift.name.get()}] $line") // null if nobody set it }

steps.say: Make the need part of the signature. The helper declares a context parameter, and so does every function that calls it, up to the place that knows the shift.
steps.code: class Shift(val name: String) // 1. the helper declares what it needs context(shift: Shift) fun note(line: String) = println("[${shift.name}] $line") // 2. callers in between declare it too, and never pass it by hand context(shift: Shift) fun printJob(jobId: String) { note("printing $jobId") }

alt.html: // Java's honest equivalent: an explicit parameter on every function in the chain record Shift(String name) {} static void note(Shift shift, String line) { System.out.println("[" + shift.name() + "] " + line); } static void printJob(Shift shift, String jobId) { note(shift, "printing " + jobId); }

steps.say: Open the context once, where the job comes in: the function that takes jobs at the counter. Forgetting it is now a compile error, no context argument for 'shift: Shift' found., instead of a [null] in the logbook.
steps.code: // 3. open the context where the shift is known fun onJobArrived(jobId: String, shiftName: String) { context(Shift(shiftName)) { printJob(jobId) } } // printJob("job-7") // error: no context argument for 'shift: Shift' found.

alt.html: void onJobArrived(String jobId, String shiftName) { printJob(new Shift(shiftName), jobId); }

steps.say: Check the price: each function in the chain gets one more JVM parameter, and nothing else. There is no ThreadLocal to look up, and the value follows the call instead of the thread, so it survives a move to another thread or into a coroutine (a task that can pause and resume, from the coroutines track).

lab.title: A contract-backed ensure and a context-aware review
steps: A JobRequest is a job as it arrives at the counter: the copies, the paper size and the file name, and the last two may be missing. Run the tests. All seven fail. Callers.kt exists for the same reason as in lesson 1: ensure is inline.
Write the body of ensure (TODO 1): throw JobRejected(code, lazyMessage()) when the condition is false. Leave the contract for later.
Write note (TODO 3) with the two context parameters, used by name.
Write review (TODO 4). Use paper.uppercase() with no !! and build: it fails on the nullable receiver.
Add the contract to ensure (TODO 2), with @OptIn(ExperimentalContracts::class) and the imports. Build again: review compiles now.
Run until all seven pass, including ReviewFromJavaTest, which calls review(logbook, shift, request, 1_000) from Java.
hints: contract { returns() implies condition; callsInPlace(lazyMessage, InvocationKind.AT_MOST_ONCE) } must be the first statement in ensure.
Inside review, copies, paper and file are properties of the receiver, so the smart cast works on paper directly.
Wrap the four ensure calls and the success note in try, and catch JobRejected to build Decision.Rejected(e.code). try is an expression, so the function can be = try { ... } catch (...) { ... }.
note(...) needs no arguments for the context: inside review, the logbook and shift context parameters are in scope, and the compiler passes them on.
lab.done: All seven tests in ReviewTest and ReviewFromJavaTest pass.

drill.title: Write ensureNotNull with a contract, from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write ensureNotNull(value, code, lazyMessage) that returns the value as non-null, throws JobRejected when it's null, and gives callers a smart cast on the variable they passed. Include the opt-in. Then write the Java version. What does the Kotlin compiler check about your contract?

answer.html: @OptIn(ExperimentalContracts::class) inline fun <T : Any> ensureNotNull(value: T?, code: String, lazyMessage: () -> String): T { contract { returns() implies (value != null) // callers get a smart cast callsInPlace(lazyMessage, InvocationKind.AT_MOST_ONCE) } if (value == null) throw JobRejected(code, lazyMessage()) return value } // it checks that contract { } comes first and warns on some callsInPlace mistakes; // it never checks that the body keeps the returns-implies promise

alt.title: Ensure.java
alt.html: static <T> T ensureNotNull(T value, String code, Supplier<String> message) { if (value == null) throw new JobRejected(code, message.get()); return value; // Java has no smart casts, so callers use the return value }

recap: The compiler never reads the body of a function you call, so your own check functions give no smart casts until they declare a contract.
returns() implies cond gives callers a smart cast after a normal return. callsInPlace(block, EXACTLY_ONCE) lets them assign a val inside the lambda.
Contracts are Experimental in Kotlin 2.4 and need @OptIn(ExperimentalContracts::class). The compiler trusts them without checking; a false one becomes a ClassCastException at run time.

Context parameters, context(shift: Shift) fun ..., replaced context receivers: a preview in Kotlin 2.2.0, Stable since 2.4.0. The compiler fills them by type from enclosing context parameters, context(...) { } blocks and implicit receivers.
On the JVM they are leading parameters (context, then receiver, then the rest), so Java passes them by hand, and adding one breaks callers that were already compiled.
The limit: a contract is believed, never checked, and a context argument is found by type, never by meaning. Explicit context arguments and callable references are not stable yet.

explain.prompt: Explain to a teammate why ensure(paper != null, "PAPER_MISSING") { ... } followed by paper.uppercase() compiles only with a contract, and what the compiler does and doesn't check about that contract.
explain.answer: The compiler decides smart casts inside one function at a time. It doesn't read the body of ensure when it compiles the caller, so without help it has no idea that ensure only returns when the condition is true, and paper stays a String?. The contract returns() implies condition, written as the first statement of ensure, is a promise stored in the Kotlin metadata: if this function returns normally, the condition holds. When the caller is compiled, the compiler reads that promise and treats paper as non-null after the call. It doesn't check the promise. If the body of ensure returned without checking, the code would still compile and fail later at run time. The compiler checks only the form: the opt-in is there, the block is the first statement, and for callsInPlace it warns about some obvious misuse such as calling the lambda twice or keeping it. So the body should be as simple as the promise, here a single if (!condition) throw.

deeper.html:
Kotlin 2.4.0 added one more Experimental contract effect, returnsResultOf(), to help the new checker for unused return values. It needs the flag -Xallow-returns-result-of, and the release notes warn that using it "produces pre-release binaries that earlier Kotlin compiler versions can't read". Keep it out of libraries that other people use.

The extended contracts from Kotlin 2.2.20 behave in an interesting way on the 2.4.21 compiler. Their old flags (-Xallow-contracts-on-more-functions and friends) now print the argument '...' is redundant for the current language version 2.4., and a generic returns(true) implies (this is Ok<T>) or a holdsIn contract compiles without any flag. So they appear to be switched on by default from language version 2.3. They still need their opt-ins, though: returnsNotNull() without @OptIn(ExperimentalExtendedContracts::class) is an opt-in error.

If you're moving code from context receivers, three differences bite. Context parameters must be named (or _), and a context parameter is not a receiver in the body, so write("x") becomes logbook.write("x"). this@Logbook is gone; use the name or contextOf<Logbook>(). And classes can't declare a context any more, only functions and properties.

Finally, a design note. The docs list "simplified dependency injection" as one use, dependency injection being a framework that builds your objects and hands each one the helpers it needs. Treat that with care. A context parameter is resolved when the code is compiled, at each call site, from what is in scope there. A dependency injection framework wires objects when the program starts, from the whole application. They answer different questions: context parameters suit values that belong to one piece of work, and constructors suit helpers that live as long as the object.
